paragraphs: The President of the United States is to be "commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States, and of the militia of the several States when called into the actual service of the United States." This provision is so obviously proper in itself, and so closely follows the precedents of the State constitutions generally, that it hardly needs explaining or defending. Even the State constitutions that elsewhere give the chief executive a council have, for the most part, placed military authority in him alone. Of all the tasks of government, directing a war calls most especially for the qualities that mark power exercised by a single hand. To direct a war is to direct the common strength, and the power to direct and employ the common strength is a usual and essential part of what we mean by the executive authority.

"The President may require the opinion, in writing, of the principal officer in each of the executive departments, upon any subject relating to the duties of their respective officers." In my view this is merely redundant in the plan, because the office would carry that right with it automatically.

He is also to be authorized to grant "reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment." Humanity and sound policy join in dictating that the merciful prerogative of pardoning should be as little restricted or hampered as possible. The criminal code of every country has so much necessary severity in it that, without easy access to exceptions in favor of unfortunate guilt, justice would wear a face too bloody and cruel. The sense of responsibility is always strongest in proportion as it is undivided. It may therefore be inferred that a single man would be most ready to attend to the force of those motives that might plead for a softening of the rigor of the law, and least likely to yield to considerations meant to shelter a fit object of its vengeance. The thought that the fate of a fellow creature depended on his sole decision would naturally inspire scrupulousness and caution. The dread of being accused of weakness or connivance would produce an equal circumspection, though of a different kind. On the other hand, since men generally draw confidence from their numbers, they might often encourage one another in an act of hardness, and might be less aware of the danger of suspicion or censure for an unwise or affected clemency. For these reasons, one man appears to be a better dispenser of the mercy of government than a body of men.

The expediency of vesting the power of pardoning in the President has, if I am not mistaken, been contested only in relation to the crime of treason. It has been urged that this power ought to have depended on the assent of one, or both, of the branches of the legislative body. I shall not deny that there are strong reasons for requiring, in this particular case, the concurrence of that body or of a part of it. Treason is a crime aimed at the very existence of the society. Once the laws have established the offender's guilt, there seems a fitness in referring the question whether an act of mercy toward him is advisable to the judgment of the legislature. This ought the more to be the case because the possibility that the chief executive himself might connive ought not to be entirely excluded. But there are also strong objections to such a plan. It is not to be doubted that a single man of prudence and good sense is better fitted, in delicate situations, to weigh the motives that may plead for and against the remission of the punishment than any numerous body whatever. It deserves particular attention that treason will often be connected with seditions that involve a large proportion of the community, as lately happened in Massachusetts. In every such case, we might expect to see the representation of the people tainted with the same spirit that had given birth to the offense. And when the parties were fairly evenly matched, the secret sympathy of the friends and supporters of the condemned person, taking advantage of the good nature and weakness of others, might frequently grant impunity where the terror of an example was necessary. On the other hand, when the sedition had arisen from causes that had inflamed the resentments of the larger party, they might often be found obstinate and unyielding when policy demanded forbearance and clemency. But the principal argument for placing the power of pardoning in this case in the chief executive is this: in times of insurrection or rebellion, there are often critical moments when a well-timed offer of pardon to the insurgents or rebels may restore the tranquillity of the commonwealth, and which, if allowed to pass unused, it may never be possible to recall afterward. The slow process of convening the legislature, or one of its branches, to obtain its sanction for the measure would frequently cause the golden opportunity to slip away. The loss of a week, a day, an hour, may sometimes be fatal. If it should be observed that a discretionary power, with a view to such contingencies, might be conferred on the President occasionally, the answer is, in the first place, that it is questionable whether, in a limited Constitution, that power could be delegated by law; and in the second place, that it would generally be unwise to take beforehand any step that might hold out the prospect of impunity. A proceeding of this kind, outside the usual course, would be likely to be read as a sign of timidity or weakness, and would tend to embolden guilt.
